rules.name: Dynamic code evaluation

message.text: Replace dynamic evaluation with explicit parsing or dispatch

rules.description: Calls that evaluate source text as code are difficult to validate and can execute unintended behavior. Prefer a data-only representation and explicit operations.

rules.name: Go data race

message.text: these exact accesses to the same Go location may execute concurrently without ordering or compatible protection

rules.description: Two ordinary Go memory accesses identify the same exact runtime location, at least one writes, their task instances may execute concurrently, and no modeled happens-before edge, compatible must-held lock, or all-atomic access pair protects them. Findings require proven and exhaustive workspace evidence; unresolved or unsupported concurrency remains open.

rules.name: Go nil dereference

message.text: this Go operation may dereference a nil value on a reachable path

rules.description: A structured pointer dereference, field access, or reviewed receiver operation is reached with an exact Nil or MaybeNil fact. Reviewed API result contracts are also retained as a nilness origin when an operation requiring a valid result occurs before its success condition is proved. Unknown scalar facts, nil-tolerant methods, and unreviewed receiver operations are not findings.

rules.name: Go failure path returns the wrong error

message.text: this exact Go API failure path returns a call that consumes a different error binding whose reaching value is nil

rules.description: A reviewed Go API reports failure through one result, but a call returned from that exact failure path consumes a different error binding whose reaching value is proven to be Go's zero value. The rule does not infer intent from names: it requires canonical API identity, exact result and binding identity, exact failure-edge control, and exhaustive reaching-definition evidence.

rules.name: Rayon parallelism inside a blocking lazy initializer

message.text: Review this blocking lazy initializer: its rayon parallelism can self-deadlock when the first call arrives on a rayon worker

rules.description: A blocking lazy-init primitive (OnceLock::get_or_init, OnceLock::get_or_try_init, Once::call_once, LazyLock::new) whose initializer closure lexically contains rayon parallelism (par_iter, into_par_iter, par_bridge, par_chunks) can self-deadlock: when the first initialization runs on a rayon worker, the initializer's parallel join steals sibling jobs, and a stolen job that re-enters the same cell parks on it forever. This is a structural review prompt, not proof of a deadlock; verify whether the cell can be reached from inside a rayon pool. Containment is lexical: a rayon call inside a nested closure defined within the initializer also matches, even when that closure only runs later. Bare rayon::join, rayon::scope, and ThreadPool::install are not matched because their unqualified names are too generic. Prefer a pool-safe memoization such as PoolSafeMemo::get_or_build_parallel, or build the value eagerly before entering the parallel region.

rules.name: Unsafe object deserialization

message.text: Replace pickle deserialization with a data-only format

rules.description: Python pickle loaders may instantiate unexpected objects. Prefer a data-only format and validate the decoded schema.

rules.name: Database call inside a loop

message.text: Review whether this lexically nested database call repeats per iteration

rules.description: A database call lexically nested under a loop can signal an N+1 pattern. This structural prompt also includes deferred nested bodies; verify execution before batching or prefetching. A for-each loop whose iterated expression provably resolves to a collection literal with at most eight elements is excluded; the proof covers declarator-established bindings (JS/TS const/let/var, Rust let, Java locals), so field-, assignment-, or call-produced iterables still report.

rules.name: Expensive operation inside nested loops

message.text: Review whether this lexically nested operation repeats across both loops

rules.description: This operation is lexically nested under two loops. The structural prompt also includes deferred nested bodies; verify execution before hoisting invariants, batching work, or reducing the iteration space. The prompt is withdrawn when the inner for-each loop's iterated expression provably resolves to a collection literal with at most eight elements, because a fixed small inner dimension makes the work linear in the outer loop rather than multiplicative; the proof covers declarator-established bindings (JS/TS const/let/var, Rust let, Java locals), so field-, assignment-, or call-produced iterables still report.

rules.name: Loop-invariant receiver sorted on every iteration

message.text: this receiver's value is established outside the enclosing loop and never re-established inside it, so every iteration re-sorts the same value; if the call sits in a closure or other deferred body, it is reported because it is written inside the loop, not because it is proven to run once per iteration

rules.description: The sorted receiver's value is established outside the enclosing loop -- its binding is declared outside and no assignment inside the loop reaches that binding -- so the loop re-sorts one unchanged-identity value on every pass. Sort once before the loop, or maintain order incrementally. Receivers that are field projections of another value are outside this rule's evidence and are not reported either way.

rules.name: Sleep inside a collection-iteration loop

message.text: Review whether this sleep throttles every iterated item

rules.description: A sleep call lexically nested under a for-each loop delays every iterated item, which can signal lockstep throttling of a whole batch. Condition-controlled while loops are excluded: a sleep there is usually the deliberate mechanism of a poll or bounded-backoff loop. This structural prompt also includes deferred nested bodies; verify execution before restructuring. A for-each loop whose iterated expression provably resolves to a collection literal with at most eight elements is also excluded; the proof covers declarator-established bindings (JS/TS const/let/var, Rust let, Java locals), so field-, assignment-, or call-produced iterables still report.
